title: The Tide of Bellbird Bay
premise: Wren Underhill, a ghostwriter who fled Bellbird Bay fifteen years ago after a betrayal she never explained, is hired to secretly write the memoirs of Marlowe Voss, a celebrated coastal novelist — and her oldest enemy. When their publisher launches an anonymous pen-pal program to 'reconnect authors with honest readers,' a clerical error pairs Wren and Marlowe with each other, and through letters that neither knows the authorship of, they begin confessing truths they could never say face-to-face. As Wren uncovers that Marlowe's bestselling debut was stolen from her late brother's journals, she must choose between exposing him and admitting her own role in the original betrayal. In the climax, on the night of the last ferry of the season, the letters are revealed, old wounds are aired before the found family of the bay, and Wren and Marlowe choose truth over safety — boarding the ferry together as partners in a co-written book and a shared life.
about_author: Paloma Thackeray spent a decade as a ghostwriter for celebrity memoirs before publishing under her own name, drawing on the strange intimacies of writing in another person's voice. She lives in a coastal town much like Bellbird Bay, where she keeps a wall of unsent letters she swears will one day become a novel.

chapters.title: The Ghost in the Manuscript
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In her Melbourne apartment, Wren finishes ghosting another celebrity memoir and receives the lucrative offer: Marlowe Voss's memoirs. Her hand shakes at his name. She accepts anyway, telling herself fifteen years is long enough for anyone to be safe. Emotional beat: dread disguised as ambition.

chapters.title: Return Ferry
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The ferry into Bellbird Bay brings back the town in fragments — the fish-and-chip shop, the boathouse, the bellbird calls. Marlowe meets her at the dock, handsome and coldly polite, and neither acknowledges their history. Emotional beat: the past arriving faster than the boat.

chapters.title: Interview One: Lying Professionally
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. First memoir session at Marlowe's cliffside house. He is charming, evasive, and controls the narrative with practiced ease. Wren notices he skips 2009 entirely — the year everything happened. Emotional beat: two professionals fencing with smiles.

chapters.title: Dear Stranger
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. The publisher's pen-pal program launches; Marlowe signs up cynically for publicity. His assigned correspondent, 'W.,' writes with startling honesty about fear and small safe lives. He answers more honestly than he means to. Emotional beat: unexpected exposure.

chapters.title: The Boathouse Regulars
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reconnects with Dot, the ferry operator, and teenage Tui, who works the chippy and has adopted Wren as an unofficial aunt. The warmth of the bay unsettles her carefully walled life. Emotional beat: belonging sneaking past defenses.

chapters.title: What the Letters Say
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Pen-pal letters deepen: 'M.' admits he built fame on something that wasn't fully his; 'W.' admits she destroyed someone once by staying silent. Each recognizes a kinship they can't name. Emotional beat: confession without consequence — yet.

chapters.title: Chapter Missing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Transcribing tapes, Wren finds Marlowe's debut novel echoes phrases from her brother Eli's journals — journals she last saw the night she left town. She confronts nothing, but starts digging. Emotional beat: suspicion hardening into grief.

chapters.title: Storm Season
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. A storm strands Marlowe and Wren at the boathouse; forced proximity cracks the professionalism. They argue about art, theft, and second chances without saying what they mean. Emotional beat: attraction sharpened by antagonism.

chapters.title: Tui's Secret
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren discovers Tui has been skipping school to write stories in Eli's old hideout. Protecting the girl forces Wren to remember protecting Eli — and how badly that ended. Emotional beat: guilt finding a new address.

chapters.title: The Letter That Knew Too Much
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren's pen-pal letter mentions a brother lost to the water; Marlowe goes white reading it. He begins suspecting who 'W.' is — and what she might know about 2009. Emotional beat: paranoia wearing tenderness's clothes.

chapters.title: Interview Seven: The Almost-Truth
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On tape, Marlowe nearly confesses the origin of his debut, then shuts off the recorder. Alone afterward, Wren finds Eli's journal hidden in his study shelf. Emotional beat: proof arriving like a slap.

chapters.title: Found Family, Fraying
chapters.summary: Dot's POV. Dot, who watched both teenagers grow up, hosts a midwinter dinner where old tensions surface. Tui asks why Wren left all those years ago; Wren can't answer. Emotional beat: love demanding honesty as its price.

chapters.title: Two Truths in One Envelope
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. Marlowe confirms his pen-pal is Wren via a phrase only she uses. Instead of exposing her, he writes back as himself-pretending-not-to-know, testing whether the honesty was real. Emotional beat: intimacy built on a fault line.

chapters.title: Eli's Last Summer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Flashback chapter: fifteen years earlier, Wren, Eli, and Marlowe were inseparable. Wren saw Marlowe take Eli's journal pages and said nothing, ashamed of her own complicity; then Eli drowned, and she fled. Emotional beat: the wound finally shown whole.

chapters.title: The Deadline
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Publisher demands the finished manuscript; the memoir's final chapter must cover 2009. Marlowe refuses to record it. Wren must decide whether to write it herself from the journal — an act of both betrayal and authorship. Emotional beat: the trap closing gently.

chapters.title: Confession by Post
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Both pen-pals, knowing now, write their truest letters: Marlowe admits the theft and that Eli's death broke him; Wren admits her silence. Neither signs a name. Emotional beat: love and ruin in the same handwriting.

chapters.title: Tui Runs
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Tui, hurt by a family rejection, disappears toward the headland in rising weather. Wren and Marlowe search together, and in the rescue Wren stops performing composure. Emotional beat: crisis stripping away the last masks.

chapters.title: What I Never Sent
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. Marlowe gives Wren a box: every letter he wrote Eli's memory over fifteen years, plus the journal pages he took — kept, he claims, because finishing Eli's story was the only way he survived. Wren doesn't believe absolution is that simple. Emotional beat: grief meeting accountability.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At the town hall, Marlowe publicly reads the true final chapter — crediting Eli Underhill as co-author of his debut — while Wren watches, unprepared for the exposure of her own secret complicity when a publisher's aide reveals the ghostwriter's identity. Emotional beat: vindication curdling into vulnerability.

chapters.title: Last Ferry Eve
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Humiliated and certain Marlowe engineered her outing, Wren packs to leave on the morning ferry. Dot and Tui plead; Marlowe waits at the dock all night in the rain. She doesn't come down. Emotional beat: the darkest hour before choice.

chapters.title: The Whole Heart
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At dawn, Wren reads his final letter aloud to herself: not asking forgiveness, only offering truth. She runs for the dock as the ferry loads, and they say the unsayable — the theft, the silence, the years — and choose each other anyway. Emotional beat: risk rewarded with reality, not fantasy.

chapters.title: Bellbird Song
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Wren's POV. One year later: their co-written book about Eli is published under three names; Tui wins a young writers' prize; Dot rings the ferry bell for no one in particular. Wren writes the last line in her own voice at last. Emotional beat: home as a verb, not a place.
